name: Location
explanation: Users should be able to tell where the current page sits within the broader structure of the site, not just what the page itself contains. Common ways to provide this are breadcrumb trails showing the path from the homepage down to the current page, a highlighted item in the main navigation showing which section is active, or a sitemap that indicates the current location. The goal is orientation: understanding how the current page relates to the rest of the site's structure, not just what's on the page itself.
whoItAffects: People with cognitive disabilities can find it difficult to build and retain a mental model of a large site's structure purely from memory, so an explicit location indicator like a breadcrumb trail helps them understand context and navigate back to a related or parent page with confidence. Screen reader users benefit from being able to query their location within a site's hierarchy, especially on large sites where the current page's relationship to other pages isn't obvious just from its own content.

codeExample.bad:
Wireless Mouse — Model X200

Product details...
codeExample.good:
1. Home
  2. Electronics
  3. Accessories
  4. Wireless Mouse — Model X200

Wireless Mouse — Model X200

Product details...

howToTest: Navigate a few levels into the site, to a product page, an article, or a subsection, and check whether anything on the page tells you where you are relative to the rest of the site: a breadcrumb trail, a highlighted section in the main navigation, or an equivalent indicator. If the page gives no clue about its place in the site's overall structure beyond its own content, this fails.

check.question: An online store's product pages show the product name, price, and description, but have no breadcrumb trail, no highlighted category in the navigation menu, and nothing else indicating which category or section of the site the product belongs to. Does this pass SC 2.4.8 Location?
choices: Yes, because the product page contains all the information a shopper needs
No, because there is no indication of the page's location within the site's overall structure
Yes, because the site's URL likely contains the category name
It depends only on whether the product has a category filter available elsewhere
